idiom_name: from/select query expressions compiled to SelectMany
implementation_notes: The compiler rewrites 'from a in A from b in B(a) select f(a, b)' into A.SelectMany(a => B(a), (a, b) => f(a, b)); any type that provides SelectMany becomes a monad with comprehension syntax, while Select is map and Where is filter. Bind is therefore a language feature for collections, options, tasks and other library types that implement the method, though the general Monad abstraction still needs a library (language-ext) because C# has no higher-kinded types. Write the query-syntax form whenever the concrete type already offers SelectMany.
code_sketch:
IEnumerable<Receipt> Receipts(Cart cart) =>
    from item in cart.Items
    from price in Lookup(item)      // SelectMany: step depends on item
    where price.Valid
    select new Receipt(item, price);
pitfalls: Query syntax only sees SelectMany/Select/Where: a type that names its bind differently cannot use it, and multiple from-clauses are easy to misread when several depend on each other.
Deferred execution: an IEnumerable query re-runs its steps on every enumeration, so side-effectful 'bind' bodies execute repeatedly.
The same LINQ operators also work on IQueryable, where the lambda becomes an expression tree translated by the provider; client-side behaviour and exceptions can differ.

variants.name: async/await over Task (continuation monad)
variants.implementation_notes: An async method is a compiler-generated continuation pipeline: each await is bind on Task<T>, resuming only after the previous task completes, and failures travel the task's faulted channel instead of the current stack. Use it for the IO instance of the pattern; keep query syntax for in-memory sequences and bridge the two only at the edges, because await is not allowed inside a query expression.
pitfalls: async void cannot be awaited or observed; use async Task everywhere except event handlers, or failures become unhandled.
Blocking on a task (.Result/.Wait/.GetAwaiter().GetResult()) in a synchronisation context deadlocks; await all the way.
Awaiting in a loop serialises independent work; use Task.WhenAll for steps that do not depend on each other.
